newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk, Jordan traders big losers in Iraq oil delay.
newsitem.headline: Turk, Jordan traders big losers in Iraq oil delay.

text.p: Turkish and Jordanian traders, chasing the lion's share of humanitarian trade with Iraq, have seen their hopes dashed after a surprise delay in the U.N. oil-for-food plan for Baghdad.

Trade with Iraq -- which has been under a U.N. embargo since its invasion of Kuwait in 1990 -- was expected to start this month with the United Nations plan for Baghdad to sell oil worth $2 billion over six months to buy food and medicine.

But earlier this week the United Nations put the plan on hold indefinitely after Iraqi government troops intervened in Kurdish factional fighting in northern Iraq, where a U.N. safe haven to protect the Kurds has been in place since 1991.

Abdulkadir Cikmaz, head of the Southeast Grain Exporters Union that has sold Iraq staples, mostly flour and pulses, worth $65 million so far this year, said Turkey's total losses from food and medicine sales after the plan's suspension would be nearly $700 million.
"We will lose $150 million from food and medicine sales to northern Iraq only, $400-$500 million from sales to Iraq itself and $50 million in pipeline transit fees," he told Reuters.
Oil traders and analysts say the plan now has an uncertain future because U.N. officials suggested a "reopening of the terms" of the plan.
Turkish trade firms, backed by trade officials, have visited Iraq several times to win a big share from Iraq's food and medicine purchases, to be worth a total of $1.3 billion.

"We were looking forward to not only the trade with Iraq under the U.N. plan but also hoping to reach trade levels we had before the Gulf crisis," said Mehmet Yildirim, head of Istanbul Chamber of Commerce.

"We do not want to be a tool for the U.S. elections. In order for U.S. leaders to increase their popularity, we are made to become losers," he told Reuters, referring to U.S. missile attacks on Iraq after the Iraqi military drive into the north.

Cikmaz said about 300 trucks carrying mostly staples and vegetable oil to northern Iraq under a U.N. humanitarian permission since 1991 have been waiting at Dohuk and Zakho since Iraqi forces attacked the Kurds last weekend.

"We now have no trade with Iraq whatsoever, it is down to zero," he said. "Turkey will also lose revenues from Mersin and Iskenderun ports that would serve the transit trade of sugar and rice into Iraq."
Turkey's state oil refiner Tupras had asked the Iraqi government to buy 2.1 million tonnes from the oil it would sell under the U.N. plan.

Turkey was earning about $300 million a year from pipeline fees before the U.N. embargo on Iraq after its invasion of Kuwait in 1990 and it was tapping Iraqi oil exports from the 986-km (616-mile) line from Kirkuk to Turkey's Ceyhan port.

The U.N. plan stipulated that most of the Iraqi oil sales be made via the pipeline, shut since the U.N. embargo on Iraq, which was Turkey's top oil supplier and third largest trade partner before the 1990-91 Gulf crisis.
Any delay in the U.N. oil-for-food deal was seen as a major blow to Jordanian traders, who were bracing for a substantial increase in trade to Iraq through the Red Sea port of Aqaba.

Aqaba's proximity to the Suez Canal makes it a natural port to unload Iraqi shipments from Europe. With better facilities than Iraq's Gulf port of Umm Qasr, it can also compete for imports from the Far East.
"It's quite a big loss to us," said one businessman who imports wheat, rice and sugar, much of it for the Iraqi market.

He said Jordanian traders had hoped that implementation of the deal could lead to an extra 100,000 tonnes of wheat, 80,000 tonnes of sugar and 50,000 tonnes of rice a month passing through Aqaba towards Iraq.
"In a small country like Jordan, those quantities can have a major impact," he said. "You employ more labourers and drivers, and the government gets substantial transit fees at the port."

Iraqi purchases of food from the new oil revenues was also expected to free up desperately needed cash for Baghdad to buy extra medicine, detergents and fertilisers -- much of which Jordanian manufacturers would be able to supply.
"Jordanian producers would have had a chance to compete internationally," the trader said. "Being neighbours, we would have an advantage."
